group.name: APT29
group.description: APT29 is threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). They have operated since at least 2008, often targeting government networks in Europe and NATO member countries, research institutes, and think tanks. APT29 reportedly compromised the Democratic National Committee starting in the summer of 2015. In April 2021, the US and UK governments attributed the SolarWinds Compromise to the SVR; public statements included citations to APT29, Cozy Bear, and The Dukes. Industry reporting also referred to the actors involved in this campaign as UNC2452, NOBELIUM, StellarParticle, Dark Halo, and SolarStorm.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.procedure: APT29 has used repeated MFA requests to gain access to victim accounts.

references.source: Suspected Russian Activity Targeting Government and Business Entities Around the Globe

T1003.002.name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.procedure: APT29 has used the `reg save` command to save registry hives.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1588.002.name: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
T1588.002.procedure: APT29 has obtained and used a variety of tools including Mimikatz, SDelete, Tor, meek, and Cobalt Strike.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1090.004.name: Proxy: Domain Fronting
T1090.004.procedure: APT29 has used the meek domain fronting plugin for Tor to hide the destination of C2 traffic.

T1528.name: Steal Application Access Token
T1528.procedure: APT29 uses stolen tokens to access victim accounts, without needing a password.

T1568.name: Dynamic Resolution
T1568.procedure: APT29 has used Dynamic DNS providers for their malware C2 infrastructure.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1068.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
T1068.procedure: APT29 has exploited CVE-2021-36934 to escalate privileges on a compromised host.

T1546.003.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
T1546.003.procedure: APT29 has used WMI event subscriptions for persistence.

T1547.001.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
T1547.001.procedure: APT29 added Registry Run keys to establish persistence.

T1136.003.procedure: APT29 can create new users through Azure AD.

T1098.005.procedure: APT29 has enrolled their own devices into compromised cloud tenants, including enrolling a device in MFA to an Azure AD environment following a successful password guessing attack against a dormant account.

T1587.003.name: Develop Capabilities: Digital Certificates
T1587.003.procedure: APT29 has created self-signed digital certificates to enable mutual TLS authentication for malware.

T1005.name: Data from Local System
T1005.procedure: APT29 has stolen data from compromised hosts.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1105.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
T1105.procedure: APT29 has downloaded additional tools and malware onto compromised networks.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1651.name: Cloud Administration Command
T1651.procedure: APT29 has used Azure Run Command and Azure Admin-on-Behalf-of (AOBO) to execute code on virtual machines.

T1566.001.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
T1566.001.procedure: APT29 has used spearphishing emails with an attachment to deliver files with exploits to initial victims.

T1078.004.name: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts
T1078.004.procedure: APT29 has gained access to a global administrator account in Azure AD and has used `Service Principal` credentials in Exchange.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1053.005.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
T1053.005.procedure: APT29 has used named and hijacked scheduled tasks to establish persistence.

T1016.001.name: System Network Configuration Discovery: Internet Connection Discovery
T1016.001.procedure: APT29 has ensured web servers in a victim environment are Internet accessible before copying tools or malware to it.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1587.001.name: Develop Capabilities: Malware
T1587.001.procedure: APT29 has used unique malware in many of their operations.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1583.006.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
T1583.006.procedure: APT29 has registered algorithmically generated Twitter handles that are used for C2 by malware, such as HAMMERTOSS. APT29 has also used legitimate web services such as Dropbox and Constant Contact in their operations.

T1090.003.name: Proxy: Multi-hop Proxy
T1090.003.procedure: A backdoor used by APT29 created a Tor hidden service to forward traffic from the Tor client to local ports 3389 (RDP), 139 (Netbios), and 445 (SMB) enabling full remote access from outside the network and has also used TOR.

T1037.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
T1037.procedure: APT29 has hijacked legitimate application-specific startup scripts to enable malware to execute on system startup.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1027.006.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: HTML Smuggling
T1027.006.procedure: APT29 has embedded an ISO file within an HTML attachment that contained JavaScript code to initiate malware execution.

T1070.004.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
T1070.004.procedure: APT29 has used SDelete to remove artifacts from victim networks.

T1203.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
T1203.procedure: APT29 has used multiple software exploits for common client software, like Microsoft Word, Exchange, and Adobe Reader, to gain code execution.

T1550.003.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
T1550.003.procedure: APT29 used Kerberos ticket attacks for lateral movement.

T1204.001.name: User Execution: Malicious Link
T1204.001.procedure: APT29 has used various forms of spearphishing attempting to get a user to click on a malicious link.

references.source: Secureworks IRON RITUAL USAID Phish May 2021

T1036.005.name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
T1036.005.procedure: APT29 has renamed malicious DLLs with legitimate names to appear benign; they have also created an Azure AD certificate with a Common Name that matched the display name of the compromised service principal.

T1110.003.name: Brute Force: Password Spraying
T1110.003.procedure: APT29 has conducted brute force password spray attacks.

T1114.002.name: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
T1114.002.procedure: APT29 has collected emails from targeted mailboxes within a compromised Azure AD tenant and compromised Exchange servers, including via Exchange Web Services (EWS) API requests.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1027.001.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding
T1027.001.procedure: APT29 used large size files to avoid detection by security solutions with hardcoded size limits.

T1556.007.name: Modify Authentication Process: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.procedure: APT29 has edited the `Microsoft.IdentityServer.Servicehost.exe.config` file to load a malicious DLL into the AD FS process, thereby enabling persistent access to any service federated with AD FS for a user with a specified User Principal Name.

T1059.001.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1059.001.procedure: APT29 has used encoded PowerShell scripts uploaded to CozyCar installations to download and install SeaDuke.

T1133.name: External Remote Services
T1133.procedure: APT29 has used compromised identities to access networks via VPNs and Citrix.

T1037.004.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: RC Scripts
T1037.004.procedure: APT29 has installed a run command on a compromised system to enable malware execution on system startup.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1021.007.name: Remote Services: Cloud Services
T1021.007.procedure: APT29 has leveraged compromised high-privileged on-premises accounts synced to Office 365 to move laterally into a cloud environment, including through the use of Azure AD PowerShell.

references.source: Mandiant Remediation and Hardening Strategies for Microsoft 365

T1595.002.name: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
T1595.002.procedure: APT29 has conducted widespread scanning of target environments to identify vulnerabilities for exploit.

T1566.002.name: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
T1566.002.procedure: APT29 has used spearphishing with a link to trick victims into clicking on a link to a zip file containing malicious files.

references.source: Secureworks IRON RITUAL USAID Phish May 2021

T1070.006.name: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
T1070.006.procedure: APT29 has used timestomping to alter the Standard Information timestamps on their web shells to match other files in the same directory.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1586.003.name: Compromise Accounts: Cloud Accounts
T1586.003.procedure: APT29 has used residential proxies, including Azure Virtual Machines, to obfuscate their access to victim environments.

T1090.002.name: Proxy: External Proxy
T1090.002.procedure: APT29 uses compromised residential endpoints as proxies for defense evasion and network access.

T1573.name: Encrypted Channel
T1573.procedure: APT29 has used multiple layers of encryption within malware to protect C2 communication.

T1047.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
T1047.procedure: APT29 used WMI to steal credentials and execute backdoors at a future time.

T1110.001.name: Brute Force: Password Guessing
T1110.001.procedure: APT29 has successfully conducted password guessing attacks against a list of mailboxes.

T1199.name: Trusted Relationship
T1199.procedure: APT29 has compromised IT, cloud services, and managed services providers to gain broad access to multiple customers for subsequent operations.

T1566.003.name: Phishing: Spearphishing via Service
T1566.003.procedure: APT29 has used the legitimate mailing service Constant Contact to send phishing e-mails.

T1078.name: Valid Accounts
T1078.procedure: APT29 has used a compromised account to access an organization's VPN infrastructure.

T1505.003.name: Server Software Component: Web Shell
T1505.003.procedure: APT29 has installed web shells on exploited Microsoft Exchange servers.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1059.006.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python
T1059.006.procedure: APT29 has developed malware variants written in Python.

T1665.name: Hide Infrastructure
T1665.procedure: APT29 uses compromised residential endpoints, typically within the same ISP IP address range, as proxies to hide the true source of C2 traffic.

T1218.005.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta
T1218.005.procedure: APT29 has use `mshta` to execute malicious scripts on a compromised host.

T1003.004.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.procedure: APT29 has used the `reg save` command to extract LSA secrets offline.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1190.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
T1190.procedure: APT29 has exploited CVE-2019-19781 for Citrix, CVE-2019-11510 for Pulse Secure VPNs, CVE-2018-13379 for FortiGate VPNs, and CVE-2019-9670 in Zimbra software to gain access.

T1553.005.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
T1553.005.procedure: APT29 has embedded ISO images and VHDX files in HTML to evade Mark-of-the-Web.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.procedure: APT29 has abused misconfigured AD CS certificate templates to impersonate admin users and create additional authentication certificates.

T1087.004.name: Account Discovery: Cloud Account
T1087.004.procedure: APT29 has conducted enumeration of Azure AD accounts.

T1098.002.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
T1098.002.procedure: APT29 has used a compromised global administrator account in Azure AD to backdoor a service principal with `ApplicationImpersonation` rights to start collecting emails from targeted mailboxes; APT29 has also used compromised accounts holding `ApplicationImpersonation` rights in Exchange to collect emails.

references.source: Mandiant APT29 Eye Spy Email Nov 22

T1078.003.name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
T1078.003.procedure: APT29 targets dormant or inactive user accounts, accounts belonging to individuals no longer at the organization but whose accounts remain on the system, for access and persistence.

T1546.008.name: Event Triggered Execution: Accessibility Features
T1546.008.procedure: APT29 used sticky-keys to obtain unauthenticated, privileged console access.

T1059.009.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Cloud API
T1059.009.procedure: APT29 has leveraged the Microsoft Graph API to perform various actions across Azure and M365 environments. They have also utilized AADInternals PowerShell Modules to access the API

T1586.002.name: Compromise Accounts: Email Accounts
T1586.002.procedure: APT29 has compromised email accounts to further enable phishing campaigns and taken control of dormant accounts.

T1204.002.name: User Execution: Malicious File
T1204.002.procedure: APT29 has used various forms of spearphishing attempting to get a user to open attachments, including, but not limited to, malicious Microsoft Word documents, .pdf, and .lnk files.

T1685.002.name: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
T1685.002.procedure: APT29 has disabled Purview Audit on targeted accounts prior to stealing emails from Microsoft 365 tenants.

T1548.002.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Bypass User Account Control

T1027.002.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
T1027.002.procedure: APT29 used UPX to pack files.

campaigns.name: Operation Ghost
campaigns.description: Operation Ghost was an APT29 campaign starting in 2013 that included operations against ministries of foreign affairs in Europe and the Washington, D.C.

T1078.002.name: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts
T1078.002.procedure: For Operation Ghost, APT29 used stolen administrator credentials for lateral movement on compromised networks.

T1102.002.name: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
T1102.002.procedure: For Operation Ghost, APT29 used social media platforms to hide communications to C2 servers.

T1001.002.name: Data Obfuscation: Steganography
T1001.002.procedure: During Operation Ghost, APT29 used steganography to hide the communications between the implants and their C&C servers.

T1583.001.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
T1583.001.procedure: For Operation Ghost, APT29 registered domains for use in C2 including some crafted to appear as existing legitimate domains.

T1587.001.name: Develop Capabilities: Malware
T1587.001.procedure: For Operation Ghost, APT29 used new strains of malware including FatDuke, MiniDuke, RegDuke, and PolyglotDuke.

T1546.003.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
T1546.003.procedure: During Operation Ghost, APT29 used WMI event subscriptions to establish persistence for malware.

T1585.001.name: Establish Accounts: Social Media Accounts
T1585.001.procedure: For Operation Ghost, APT29 registered Twitter accounts to host C2 nodes.

T1027.003.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Steganography
T1027.003.procedure: During Operation Ghost, APT29 used steganography to hide payloads inside valid images.

campaigns.name: SolarWinds Compromise
campaigns.description: The SolarWinds Compromise was a sophisticated supply chain cyber operation conducted by APT29 that was discovered in mid-December 2020.

T1606.002.name: Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 created tokens using compromised SAML signing certificates.

references.source: Microsoft - Customer Guidance on Recent Nation-State Cyber Attacks

T1078.004.name: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts
T1078.004.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used a compromised O365 administrator account to create a new Service Principal.

T1053.005.name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
T1053.005.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used `scheduler` and `schtasks` to create new tasks on remote host as part of their lateral movement. They manipulated scheduled tasks by updating an existing legitimate task to execute their tools and then returned the scheduled task to its original configuration. APT29 also created a scheduled task to maintain SUNSPOT persistence when the host booted.

T1087.002.name: Account Discovery: Domain Account
T1087.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used PowerShell to discover domain accounts by exectuing `Get-ADUser` and `Get-ADGroupMember`.

T1090.001.name: Proxy: Internal Proxy
T1090.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used SSH port forwarding capabilities on public-facing systems, and configured at least one instance of Cobalt Strike to use a network pipe over SMB.

T1114.002.name: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
T1114.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 collected emails from specific individuals, such as executives and IT staff, using `New-MailboxExportRequest` followed by `Get-MailboxExportRequest`.

T1069.002.name: Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups
T1069.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used AdFind to enumerate domain groups.

T1057.name: Process Discovery
T1057.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used multiple command-line utilities to enumerate running processes.

T1584.001.name: Compromise Infrastructure: Domains
T1584.001.procedure: For the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 compromised domains to use for C2.

T1016.001.name: System Network Configuration Discovery: Internet Connection Discovery
T1016.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used GoldFinder to perform HTTP GET requests to check internet connectivity and identify HTTP proxy servers and other redirectors that an HTTP request travels through.

T1550.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
T1550.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used forged SAML tokens that allowed the actors to impersonate users and bypass MFA, enabling APT29 to access enterprise cloud applications and services.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 stole users' saved passwords from Chrome.

T1078.002.name: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts
T1078.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used domain administrators' accounts to help facilitate lateral movement on compromised networks.

T1036.005.name: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
T1036.005.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 renamed software and DLLs with legitimate names to appear benign.

T1665.name: Hide Infrastructure
T1665.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 set the hostnames of their C2 infrastructure to match legitimate hostnames in the victim environment. They also used IP addresses originating from the same country as the victim for their VPN infrastructure.

T1098.002.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
T1098.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 added their own devices as allowed IDs for active sync using `Set-CASMailbox`, allowing it to obtain copies of victim mailboxes. It also added additional permissions (such as Mail.Read and Mail.ReadWrite) to compromised Application or Service Principals.

references.source: Microsoft - Customer Guidance on Recent Nation-State Cyber Attacks

T1021.001.name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
T1021.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used RDP sessions from public-facing systems to internal servers.

T1213.name: Data from Information Repositories
T1213.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 accessed victims' internal knowledge repositories (wikis) to view sensitive corporate information on products, services, and internal business operations.

T1021.002.name: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
T1021.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used administrative accounts to connect over SMB to targeted users.

T1059.005.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
T1059.005.procedure: For the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 wrote malware such as Sibot in Visual Basic.

T1568.name: Dynamic Resolution
T1568.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used dynamic DNS resolution to construct and resolve to randomly-generated subdomains for C2.

T1589.001.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Credentials
T1589.001.procedure: For the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 conducted credential theft operations to obtain credentials to be used for access to victim environments.

T1552.004.name: Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys
T1552.004.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 obtained PKI keys, certificate files, and the private encryption key from an Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) container to decrypt corresponding SAML signing certificates.

T1587.001.name: Develop Capabilities: Malware
T1587.001.procedure: For the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used numerous pieces of malware that were likely developed for or by the group, including SUNBURST, SUNSPOT, Raindrop, and TEARDROP.

T1140.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
T1140.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used 7-Zip to decode their Raindrop malware.

T1005.name: Data from Local System
T1005.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 extracted files from compromised networks.

T1685.001.name: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Windows Event Log
T1685.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29, used `AUDITPOL` to prevent the collection of audit logs.

T1083.name: File and Directory Discovery
T1083.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 obtained information about the configured Exchange virtual directory using `Get-WebServicesVirtualDirectory`.

T1069.name: Permission Groups Discovery
T1069.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used the `Get-ManagementRoleAssignment` PowerShell cmdlet to enumerate Exchange management role assignments through an Exchange Management Shell.

T1018.name: Remote System Discovery
T1018.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used AdFind to enumerate remote systems.

T1021.006.name: Remote Services: Windows Remote Management
T1021.006.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used WinRM via PowerShell to execute commands and payloads on remote hosts.

T1550.001.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
T1550.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used compromised service principals to make changes to the Office 365 environment.

T1098.003.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles
T1098.003.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 granted `company administrator` privileges to a newly created service principle.

T1553.002.name: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
T1553.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 was able to get SUNBURST signed by SolarWinds code signing certificates by injecting the malware into the SolarWinds Orion software lifecycle.

T1218.011.name: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
T1218.011.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used `Rundll32.exe` to execute payloads.

references.source: Microsoft - Customer Guidance on Recent Nation-State Cyber Attacks

T1546.003.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
T1546.003.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used a WMI event filter to invoke a command-line event consumer at system boot time to launch a backdoor with `rundll32.exe`.

T1190.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
T1190.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 exploited CVE-2020-0688 against the Microsoft Exchange Control Panel to regain access to a network.

T1213.003.name: Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
T1213.003.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 downloaded source code from code repositories.

T1686.name: Disable or Modify System Firewall
T1686.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used `netsh` to configure firewall rules that limited certain UDP outbound packets.

T1059.001.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1059.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used PowerShell to create new tasks on remote machines, identify configuration settings, exfiltrate data, and execute other commands.

T1070.004.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
T1070.004.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 routinely removed their tools, including custom backdoors, once remote access was achieved.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 stole Chrome browser cookies by copying the Chrome profile directories of targeted users.

T1606.001.name: Forge Web Credentials: Web Cookies
T1606.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 bypassed MFA set on OWA accounts by generating a cookie value from a previously stolen secret key.

T1550.004.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
T1550.004.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used stolen cookies to access cloud resources and a forged `duo-sid` cookie to bypass MFA set on an email account.

T1074.002.name: Data Staged: Remote Data Staging
T1074.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 staged data and files in password-protected archives on a victim's OWA server.

T1098.005.name: Account Manipulation: Device Registration
T1098.005.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 registered devices in order to enable mailbox syncing via the `Set-CASMailbox` command.

T1133.name: External Remote Services
T1133.procedure: For the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used compromised identities to access networks via SSH, VPNs, and other remote access tools.

T1199.name: Trusted Relationship
T1199.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 gained access through compromised accounts at cloud solution partners, and used compromised certificates issued by Mimecast to authenticate to Mimecast customer systems.

T1059.003.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
T1059.003.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used `cmd.exe` to execute commands on remote machines.

T1070.006.name: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
T1070.006.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 modified timestamps of backdoors to match legitimate Windows files.

T1558.003.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 obtained Ticket Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Active Directory Service Principle Names to crack offline.

T1680.name: Local Storage Discovery
T1680.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used `fsutil` to check available free space before executing actions that might create large files on disk.

T1685.name: Disable or Modify Tools
T1685.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used the service control manager on a remote system to disable services associated with security monitoring products.

T1105.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
T1105.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 downloaded additional malware, such as TEARDROP and Cobalt Strike, onto a compromised host following initial access.

T1078.003.name: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
T1078.003.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used compromised local accounts to access victims' networks.

T1070.name: Indicator Removal
T1070.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 temporarily replaced legitimate utilities with their own, executed their payload, and then restored the original file.

T1003.006.name: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
T1003.006.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used privileged accounts to replicate directory service data with domain controllers.

T1036.004.name: Masquerading: Masquerade Task or Service
T1036.004.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 named tasks `\Microsoft\Windows\SoftwareProtectionPlatform\EventCacheManager` in order to appear legitimate.

T1098.001.name: Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials
T1098.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 added credentials to OAuth Applications and Service Principals.

references.source: Microsoft - Customer Guidance on Recent Nation-State Cyber Attacks

T1482.name: Domain Trust Discovery
T1482.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used the `Get-AcceptedDomain` PowerShell cmdlet to enumerate accepted domains through an Exchange Management Shell. They also used AdFind to enumerate domains and to discover trust between federated domains.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used account credentials they obtained to attempt access to Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) passwords.

T1047.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
T1047.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used WMI for the remote execution of files for lateral movement.

T1195.002.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
T1195.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 gained initial network access to some victims via a trojanized update of SolarWinds Orion software.

T1070.008.name: Indicator Removal: Clear Mailbox Data
T1070.008.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 removed evidence of email export requests using `Remove-MailboxExportRequest`.

T1484.002.name: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Trust Modification
T1484.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 changed domain federation trust settings using Azure AD administrative permissions to configure the domain to accept authorization tokens signed by their own SAML signing certificate.

T1583.001.name: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
T1583.001.procedure: For the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 acquired C2 domains, sometimes through resellers.

T1087.name: Account Discovery
T1087.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 obtained a list of users and their roles from an Exchange server using `Get-ManagementRoleAssignment`.

T1078.name: Valid Accounts
T1078.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used different compromised credentials for remote access and to move laterally.

T1560.001.name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
T1560.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used 7-Zip to compress stolen emails into password-protected archives prior to exfltration; APT29 also compressed text files into zipped archives.

T1048.002.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
T1048.002.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 exfiltrated collected data over a simple HTTPS request to a password-protected archive staged on a victim's OWA servers.

T1071.001.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
T1071.001.procedure: During the SolarWinds Compromise, APT29 used HTTP for C2 and data exfiltration.
